challenges.name: cache-drift-duplicate-events-evidence
challenges.title: Cache Drift & Duplicate Events: read the evidence
challenges.description: Learners see their leaderboard score go backwards while PostgreSQL holds the right total. Six statements on one evidence pack - the consumer log (A), the leaderboard API and learner_score (B), Redis MONITOR and INFO (C) and the consumer code (D) - take you from reading the evidence to a hypothesis, past two wrong explanations, to the fix and how to prove it.

questions.question:
Evidence A - lb-consumer log, 2026-10-26 (UTC), learner u_2041:
10:00:01.204 consumer-1 recv evt_a91 user=u_2041 total=1180 v=16 attempt=1
10:00:01.209 consumer-1 ZADD lb:global 1180 u_2041, ack evt_a91
10:00:01.958 consumer-1 recv evt_b07 user=u_2041 total=1240 v=17 attempt=1
10:00:01.962 consumer-1 ZADD lb:global 1240 u_2041
10:00:01.963 consumer-1 SIGTERM (deploy 2026.10.26-2): exiting, not acked: evt_b07
10:00:03.115 consumer-2 recv evt_c55 user=u_2041 total=1310 v=18 attempt=1
10:00:03.118 consumer-2 ZADD lb:global 1310 u_2041, ack evt_c55
10:00:05.401 consumer-2 recv evt_b07 user=u_2041 total=1240 v=17 attempt=2 (redelivered: ack deadline 3 s passed)
10:00:05.405 consumer-2 ZADD lb:global 1240 u_2041, ack evt_b07

Evidence C - redis-cli MONITOR (excerpt) and INFO server:
1793008801.209000 [0 10.0.3.21:51022] "ZADD" "lb:global" "1180" "u_2041"
1793008801.962000 [0 10.0.3.21:51022] "ZADD" "lb:global" "1240" "u_2041"
1793008803.118000 [0 10.0.3.22:40318] "ZADD" "lb:global" "1310" "u_2041"
1793008803.420000 [0 10.0.3.23:38804] "ZADD" "lb:global" "1025" "u_3307"
1793008803.591000 [0 10.0.3.22:40318] "ZADD" "lb:global" "990" "u_3307"
1793008805.405000 [0 10.0.3.22:40318] "ZADD" "lb:global" "1240" "u_2041"
uptime_in_seconds:1843215

Statement: "evt_b07 was written to Redis twice: consumer-1 wrote 1240 before it exited without acknowledging the message, and consumer-2 wrote 1240 again when the queue redelivered it at 10:00:05."
questions.explanation: True. Log A shows consumer-1 running the ZADD for evt_b07 at 10:00:01.962 and exiting one millisecond later with evt_b07 not acknowledged; after the 3-second ack deadline the queue gives the message to consumer-2 with attempt=2. MONITOR (C) shows both writes, from two client addresses. This is at-least-once delivery working as designed: the consumer acknowledges after it processes, so a crash or a restart between the two means the message is processed again. The common misconception is that a queue delivers each message exactly once; it does not promise that, and the consumer has to cope.

Evidence D - the consumer (workers/leaderboard-consumer.ts):
queue.consume("score.updated", { prefetch: 10, ackDeadlineSeconds: 3 }, async (msg) => {
  const event = JSON.parse(msg.body) as ScoreUpdated; // { eventId, userId, total, version }
  await redis.zadd("lb:global", event.total, event.userId);
  await msg.ack();
});

Statement: "u_2041 went from 1310 back to 1240 because the consumer writes each event's total with ZADD in the order the messages arrive, so the redelivered version 17 overwrote version 18: the last write wins."
questions.explanation: True. The consumer in D never compares anything: whatever arrives is written. ZADD on an existing member replaces its score, so the sorted set always holds the total of the last delivery, not of the newest event. Version 18 (1310) was written at 10:00:03.118 and the late copy of version 17 (1240) at 10:00:05.405, so 1240 stayed. The hypothesis explains every piece of evidence: the redelivery in A, the order of writes in C, the drop in rank in B and the correct row in PostgreSQL, which never saw the redelivery. The misconception is to think a write of a total is safe to repeat in any order; it is safe to repeat, not safe to reorder.

uptime_in_seconds:1843215

Statement: "Redis lost the 1310 write: it restarted and reloaded an older snapshot, which is why ZSCORE lb:global u_2041 now returns 1240."
questions.explanation: False. INFO says uptime_in_seconds:1843215, about 21 days, so Redis did not restart during the incident and loaded no snapshot. MONITOR shows an explicit ZADD lb:global 1240 u_2041 at 10:00:05.405 from 10.0.3.22, the address of consumer-2: Redis stored exactly what it was told. PostgreSQL still holds 1310 at version 18 because the database never received the late event. Lost writes after a restart are a real risk (lesson 4.3 covers persistence), but blaming storage without checking uptime and MONITOR sends the team to the wrong fix. The process that restarted here was the consumer, not Redis.

Statement: "The clocks of api-1 and api-2 are skewed, so Redis sorted the two ZADD commands for u_3307 by the wrong timestamp; syncing the hosts with NTP would stop the score from going backwards."
questions.explanation: False. Redis does not order commands by any client timestamp: it executes them in the order they arrive, and MONITOR, stamped by Redis's own clock, shows 1025 written before 990. The consumer in D does not read published or any other time either, so no clock can be to blame. The order that matters is the version from learner_score: 9 is older than 10, and that counter comes from one row in one database, independent of any host clock. evt_e31 was simply processed after evt_e40 because two consumers work in parallel. That is also why the fix compares versions rather than timestamps: ordering by wall-clock time across hosts is exactly what clock skew can break.

False. It fixes u_2041, because the late write was a redelivery of the same message (evt_b07), whose id would already be marked. It does not fix u_3307: evt_e40 (version 10) and evt_e31 (version 9) are two different events, each delivered once, and the older one simply arrived last. Stopping that needs a version check: apply an event only if its version is higher than the version last applied for that learner (for example a field in the hash lb:version), and never let a stale event decrease the score. The common misconception is that idempotency also gives ordering. The two checks answer different questions: is this the same message again, and is this message older than what I already have.

Statement: "A replay test that feeds the six logged deliveries, in the logged order and with a consumer restart after evt_b07's first delivery, to the consumer on an empty Redis and then compares ZSCORE lb:global with learner_score.total for both learners, fails on the current consumer and passes after the fix."
questions.explanation: True. On the current consumer the replay ends with u_2041 at 1240 and u_3307 at 990, while learner_score says 1310 and 1025, so the comparison fails. After the fix the redelivery of evt_b07 is skipped as a duplicate and evt_e31 as stale, and both scores match the database. The restart in the replay matters: a fix that remembers ids or versions in the consumer's memory forgets them on restart and fails, while state kept in Redis survives. Comparing Redis with the source of truth, not eyeballing the leaderboard, is the verification; the same comparison, run on a sample of learners every few minutes in production, is the drift alarm.

challenges.name: duplicate-out-of-order-events
challenges.title: Duplicate & Out-of-order Events
challenges.description:
Learners on the CodeDev leaderboard watch their score go backwards: u_2041 had 1310 points at 10:00:03 and 1240 at 10:00:05, while learner_score in PostgreSQL still says 1310 at version 18. The queue delivers score.updated messages at least once and in any order: a consumer restart redelivers every message that was not acknowledged, for up to 24 hours, and two consumers share the queue. ScoreConsumer.handle writes the total of every delivered event with ZADD, so whichever delivery arrives last wins.

Fix ScoreConsumer.handle(raw), which is called once per delivery and returns one outcome:
- "invalid": parseEvent returned null. Write nothing (the starter already does this).
- "duplicate": this eventId was already processed. Write nothing. Remember processed ids in Redis under the key lb:seen:<eventId> with a TTL of 48 hours (172800 seconds), twice the 24-hour redelivery window; a marker without a TTL would stay in Redis forever. The runner creates a new ScoreConsumer on every restart, so anything kept in the object is lost.
- "stale": the learner already has an applied event with the same or a higher version. Leave the score as it is.
- "applied": otherwise. ZADD the event's total to lb:global and remember this version for the learner (for example in the hash lb:version). A newer version can carry a lower total (a correction after a plagiarism review): it must be applied.
Mark every event that is not invalid as processed, whether it was applied or stale.

A message is { eventId, userId, total, version }; version is learner_score.version, which starts at 1 and grows by 1 on every change of that learner's total. Use the FakeRedis in the file (get, set with { ex, nx }, del, exists, expire, ttl, hset, hget, hgetall, zadd, zscore, zrevrange, zcard); time comes from a fake clock.

Input (stdin, JSON): { "trace": boolean, "steps": [...] } with up to 1,000 steps. A step is { "deliver": <message> }, { "restart": true } or { "advanceSeconds": n }.
Output: with trace, one line per step (the outcome and ZSCORE after it); then the outcome counts, the top 10 of lb:global (highest score first, ties by member descending), the drift against PostgreSQL (learners whose ZSCORE differs from the total of their highest delivered version) and the number of live lb:seen:* keys.
hints: Two different things go wrong in the incident: the same message arrives twice, and an older event arrives after a newer one. Which field of an event says "this is the same message", and which says "this is older than what I already have"? Where must that memory live so a restart does not erase it?

Look at handle: it calls ZADD before it asks Redis anything. Before writing you need two reads - does lb:seen:<eventId> exist, and which version was last applied for event.userId - and the outcome follows from them in that order. Then check the TTL you give the marker against the 24-hour redelivery window, and run the starter's trace on the public tests to see where ZSCORE goes down.

A similar case on other data: an order-status consumer gets { eventId, orderId, status, seq }. It skips a message whose id is already marked in orders:seen:<id> (marker TTL longer than its queue's redelivery window), keeps the last applied seq per order in a hash, ignores a message whose seq is not higher than the stored one, and marks the id either way. Delivering seq 3, seq 2, then seq 3 again gives applied, stale, duplicate, and the order keeps the status of seq 3.
